title: Why two companies: the creditor wall
summary: Splitting a business into an operating company that takes the risk and a holding company that keeps the value builds a wall between creditors and accumulated wealth. This lesson explains how the wall works and the ways it is commonly breached.
body:
Bottom line. An operating company, called an Opco, does the risky work: it signs contracts, hires people and can be sued. A holding company, called a Holdco, owns the Opco's shares and keeps the surplus cash and assets. Moving value up to the Holdco puts it behind a wall that the Opco's creditors usually cannot climb. The wall only holds if it is built properly and not breached by your own signatures.

In plain English

Mr Shabazz, think of a construction site. You keep the tools in use on site, and you lock the rest in a separate yard. If something on site is damaged or seized, the yard is untouched. A Holdco is that separate yard.

The Opco faces the outside world. A contractor with a defect claim, a supplier owed money, an injured worker or a tenant in a dispute will sue the Opco. If the Opco's profits have already been moved up to the Holdco, those profits are not the Opco's assets any more. As a general rule, the Opco's creditors can only take the Opco's assets.

Developers often add a third kind of company, a property company, sometimes called a Propco, that owns a single piece of land. Each project in its own company means a problem in one project does not reach the land in another.

The framework

  1. Who owns what. The individual, or a family trust, owns the Holdco. The Holdco owns the Opco and any Propcos. Each company has its own name, accounts and records.
  2. Move value up regularly. Surplus cash leaves the Opco by dividend or another documented method, usually while the Opco is healthy. The next lesson covers the tax side.
  3. Pass the solvency test first. Corporate statutes forbid paying a dividend if the company would then be unable to pay its debts as they fall due, or if its assets would fall below its liabilities and stated capital. The federal rule is in section 42 of the Canada Business Corporations Act. Directors who approve an improper dividend can be personally liable.
  4. Know the clawback rules. Insolvency law can reverse transfers made at an undervalue, or made to favour one creditor, within set periods before a bankruptcy. In Canada these are in the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, sections 95 and 96. Value moved up while the Opco is healthy, and documented, is far safer than value moved up when trouble is visible.
  5. Do not breach the wall yourself. If the Holdco guarantees the Opco's bank loan, or pledges its assets as security, then for that lender there is no wall. Lenders often ask for exactly this.
  6. Keep the companies separate in practice. Separate bank accounts, books and contracts. Lesson 20 covers this in detail.

A worked example

Hypothetical. A developer's Opco is a general contractor. Over three profitable years it builds up 500,000 of surplus cash. In year three, while solvent and with its books showing it can pay its debts, it pays a documented dividend of 400,000 to its Holdco, approved by a directors' resolution that records the solvency test.

In year five, a building the Opco built has a defect. The owner sues the Opco and wins 700,000. The Opco has 150,000 in assets. As a general rule, the claimant can collect the 150,000 from the Opco but cannot reach the 400,000 in the Holdco, because the Holdco did not do the work and is a separate person.

Now change one fact. Suppose the Holdco had guaranteed the Opco's obligations under that construction contract. Then the owner could pursue the Holdco under the guarantee, and the wall would be gone for this claim.

Change a different fact. Suppose the 400,000 had been moved in year five, the week after the defect was discovered. A court may look closely at a transfer made when a claim was already visible.

Professional Sign-Off Required: corporate counsel for the structure and dividend resolutions, and a tax advisor before any dividend is paid.

The beginner mistake

Setting up a Holdco and then never moving anything into it, so the Opco keeps all the cash at risk. The opposite mistake is moving cash up only when trouble arrives, which is exactly when the transfer is most likely to be challenged. A third mistake is having the Holdco sign guarantees for every Opco obligation, which takes the wall down from the inside.

How you will use it

Draw your structure on one page: who owns each company, what each one does, which assets each holds, and which guarantees run between them. Each line of risk should end in the company that carries that risk.

Then make moving surplus a routine, not a reaction. After each year-end, ask your accountant how much the Opco can safely move up, pass the solvency test in a signed resolution, and move it. Keep a register of every guarantee or security one company has given for another, and negotiate to remove them as projects stabilise.

Finally, put each new project in its own company before you sign the purchase agreement. Moving land into a company after the fact can trigger tax and fees that are easy to avoid at the start.
checklist: Draw the structure: owners, companies, assets and guarantees.
Keep risky activity in the Opco and surplus in the Holdco.
Move surplus up regularly while the Opco is healthy.
Record the solvency test in a signed resolution before each dividend.
Keep a register of guarantees between companies and remove them when possible.
Put each new project in its own company before signing.
Get tax advice before moving any value between companies.

selftest.q: Your Opco has 600,000 of cash. A former client has just sent a letter threatening a 300,000 claim. You want to move 500,000 to your Holdco today. What are the risks?
selftest.a: Moving a large amount right after a claim becomes visible is the riskiest time to do it. If the Opco later cannot pay the claim, the transfer may be examined under insolvency rules on undervalue transfers and preferences, and the directors who approved a dividend that failed the solvency test can face personal liability. Before moving anything, have the claim assessed, confirm the Opco remains solvent after the transfer with the claim taken into account, document the solvency test, and get advice on the tax and timing. The better practice was to move surplus regularly in earlier, calm years. Professional Sign-Off Required: corporate counsel and a tax advisor.

apply: Draw your current company structure on one page. Mark where your surplus cash sits today and list every guarantee one of your companies has given for another.
sources: Canada Business Corporations Act, RSC 1985, c C-44, section 42 (dividend solvency test). Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, RSC 1985, c B-3, sections 95 and 96 (preferences and transfers at undervalue). Provincial corporate statutes, including Alberta's Business Corporations Act, RSA 2000, c B-9, contain similar solvency tests [Alberta section number unverified — confirm independently]. Section references are cited from the author's working knowledge and should be read on the official Justice Laws website, in the current consolidation, before being relied on. All figures are hypothetical. Education only.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: corporate counsel for the structure and dividend resolutions, and a tax advisor before any dividend is paid.

title: Moving value upstream: intercorporate dividends (concepts)
summary: In Canada, many dividends paid from one Canadian company to another can move up a structure with little or no immediate corporate tax, which is why a Holdco works. This lesson explains the concept and the main rules that can switch that treatment off, at a level suitable for a briefing to your tax advisor.
body:
Bottom line. In Canada, a taxable dividend paid by one Canadian company to another is generally deductible by the company that receives it, so profit can often move from Opco to Holdco without a second layer of corporate tax. But special taxes and anti-avoidance rules can apply, and they depend on facts your tax advisor must check. Learn the concepts so you can ask the right questions. Do not apply them without sign-off.

In plain English

Mr Shabazz, profit inside a company has usually already been taxed at the corporate level. If moving it from one of your companies to another taxed it again, a Holdco structure would be expensive to use. Canadian tax law generally avoids that. When a taxable Canadian corporation pays a taxable dividend to another taxable Canadian corporation, the receiving company can usually deduct the dividend when computing its taxable income. The rule is in section 112 of the Income Tax Act (Canada).

The result is that, in the ordinary case, the Opco pays tax on its profit once, and the after-tax profit can move up to the Holdco without being taxed again in the Holdco. Personal tax is paid later, when money finally leaves the Holdco and reaches an individual.

That is the concept. The rest of this lesson is about the rules that make it more complicated, because each one can turn a routine dividend into a tax bill.

The framework

  1. Corporate law first. A dividend must be declared by the directors and must pass the solvency test in the corporate statute. Tax treatment never fixes a dividend that was not properly declared.
  2. The intercorporate deduction. The receiving corporation generally deducts the dividend under section 112 of the Income Tax Act (Canada). That is what lets value move upstream.
  3. Part IV tax. A private corporation that receives certain dividends can owe a special refundable tax, called Part IV tax, under section 186 of the Act. Whether it applies depends on whether the two companies are connected, which broadly means control or a significant shareholding, and on whether the paying company received a tax refund when it paid the dividend. Part IV tax is refundable when the receiving company itself later pays dividends, so it is often a timing cost rather than a permanent one [details unverified — confirm independently].
  4. The capital gains rule. Section 55 of the Act contains an anti-avoidance rule, in subsection 55(2), that can treat an intercorporate dividend as a capital gain instead of a deductible dividend. Broadly, it targets dividends that reduce a gain on shares beyond the income earned on those shares after a certain date, a figure advisors call safe income. Large dividends paid before a sale or a reorganisation are where this rule most often matters.
  5. Timing and records. Record the declaration, the amount, the date and the solvency test in a resolution, and make sure the payment actually moves, or is properly recorded as owing.

A worked example

Hypothetical. An Opco earns 500,000 of active business income in a year, pays its corporate tax, and has 400,000 of after-tax profit. It is wholly owned by the developer's Holdco.

The directors confirm the Opco is solvent, declare a 300,000 dividend, and pay it to the Holdco. In the ordinary case, the Holdco deducts the 300,000 under section 112, and there is no immediate corporate tax in the Holdco on that dividend. The 300,000 now sits behind the creditor wall described in the previous lesson.

Now change the facts. Suppose the Opco is about to be sold, and the plan is to pay a 1,000,000 dividend first so that the sale price, and the gain, are lower. That is the kind of situation where subsection 55(2) may treat part of the dividend as a capital gain instead. Whether it does depends on the safe income on the shares, which needs a calculation by a tax advisor.

Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor before any intercorporate dividend is declared, and corporate counsel for the resolution.

The beginner mistake

Assuming that "dividends between my companies are tax free" in every case. In the ordinary case they often are not taxed again, but Part IV tax and the capital gains rule are exactly the traps that catch owners who do not check. A second mistake is paying a dividend that was never properly declared, or that failed the solvency test, and trying to fix it later.

How you will use it

Use these concepts to brief your tax advisor before each year-end, not to make the decision yourself. Bring four facts: how much surplus the Opco has after tax; whether the Opco received or will receive a dividend refund; whether any sale, reorganisation or new investor is planned in the next few years; and how much cash the Opco must keep to operate safely.

Then ask three questions. How much can move up this year without unexpected tax? Does Part IV tax apply, and when will it be refunded? Is any part of this dividend exposed to subsection 55(2)? With those answers, you sign the resolution knowing what it does, instead of learning about it from a reassessment.
checklist: Confirm the dividend is properly declared and passes the solvency test.
Ask whether the intercorporate deduction applies in the ordinary way.
Ask whether Part IV tax applies and when it would be refunded.
Ask whether any part of the dividend is exposed to subsection 55(2).
Tell your advisor about any planned sale, reorganisation or new investor.
Record the declaration, amount, date and payment.

selftest.q: You plan to sell your Opco next year. Your plan is to have the Opco pay your Holdco a large dividend first, to strip out the cash before the sale. What should you raise with your tax advisor?
selftest.a: This is the situation where the capital gains rule in subsection 55(2) of the Income Tax Act (Canada) is most likely to matter, because a large pre-sale dividend may reduce the gain on the shares. Ask your advisor to calculate the safe income on the shares, to confirm how much can be paid as a dividend without being recharacterised as a capital gain, and to check whether Part IV tax applies. Also confirm the Opco remains solvent after the dividend, and tell the buyer's side early, because a pre-sale dividend affects the price and the deal documents. Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor and corporate counsel.

apply: Before your next year-end, write a short brief for your tax advisor with the four facts listed in this lesson and the three questions. Send it a month before the year-end, not after.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada), RSC 1985, c 1 (5th Supp), section 112 (intercorporate dividend deduction), section 186 (Part IV tax) and subsection 55(2) (dividends treated as capital gains), named at the level of concepts only; the detailed conditions, including the meaning of connected corporations and safe income, are complex, change over time and are tagged for independent confirmation where described. Corporate solvency tests are in the governing corporate statute. Section references are cited from the author's working knowledge and should be read on the official Justice Laws website, in the current consolidation, before being relied on. All figures are hypothetical. Education only.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor before any intercorporate dividend is declared, and corporate counsel for the resolution.

title: Lending between related companies and documenting it
summary: Money lent between your own companies is a real loan in law and in tax, and it needs to be documented as one: an agreement, terms, approvals and, where it matters, security. Undocumented transfers create tax risk, lender problems and disputes about whether money was a loan at all.
body:
Bottom line. When one of your companies lends money to another, treat it exactly as you would a loan to a stranger. Write a loan agreement, set the interest and repayment terms, approve it by resolution, take security if it matters, and record it in both sets of books. An undocumented transfer is not clearly a loan, and in a dispute or a tax review that uncertainty costs money.

In plain English

Mr Shabazz, in a group of companies, money moves around. The Holdco has cash and a new Propco needs a deposit. One project company has surplus and another is waiting for a construction draw. It is tempting to transfer the money and sort it out later.

The problem is that "later" is often a lender's review, a tax review, a sale, a dispute between co-owners, or an insolvency. At that point, everyone asks the same questions. Was this a loan, a gift, a dividend or a capital contribution? What interest was agreed? When is it repayable? Is it secured? If there is no document, the answers become arguments.

A documented loan also does something useful. If the Holdco lends to the Opco and takes security, the Holdco can stand as a secured creditor of the Opco. If the Opco fails, a secured lender is generally paid from the secured assets before unsecured creditors. That can protect value you have already moved up.

The framework

  1. The loan agreement. A written agreement, or at least a promissory note, which is a signed promise to repay a stated sum. It should set the amount, the interest rate, how interest is paid, when the principal is repaid, whether it is repayable on demand, and what counts as default.
  2. Approval. A directors' resolution in each company approving the loan. Where the same person is a director of both, record the disclosure of that interest.
  3. Security. If the loan matters, take security. A general security agreement covers the borrower's personal property, such as equipment, receivables and cash. A mortgage covers land. Security over personal property is usually registered in a provincial personal property registry to be effective against other creditors. Ask counsel which registrations apply.
  4. The bank's position. The borrower's bank will usually require the related lender to postpone, meaning agree to be repaid after the bank, or subordinate its security. Read those documents, because they decide when you can be repaid.
  5. Tax. Interest paid is generally deductible by the borrower only if the borrowed money is used to earn income from a business or property, under paragraph 20(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act (Canada). Interest received is income to the lender. Loans from a company to a shareholder who is an individual are different and have their own rules, including subsection 15(2) and section 80.4 of the Act.
  6. Books. Record the loan the same way in both companies, with matching balances, and reconcile them at every year-end.

A worked example

Hypothetical. A developer's Holdco has 400,000 of cash. A new Propco needs 300,000 to complete a land purchase. The Holdco lends 300,000 to the Propco at 6 percent a year, which is 18,000 of interest a year, repayable in three years, secured by a general security agreement registered in the personal property registry and a second mortgage on the land.

Both boards sign resolutions. The developer, who is a director of both companies, records the interest in each. The Propco's construction lender later requires the Holdco to postpone its mortgage behind the bank's first mortgage. The Holdco agrees, but negotiates that interest can still be paid while the bank loan is in good standing.

Two years later the project goes badly and the land sells for less than expected. The bank is repaid first. The Holdco, as a registered secured creditor, ranks ahead of the Propco's unsecured suppliers for what is left. Had the 300,000 been an undocumented transfer, the Holdco might have ranked with the unsecured creditors, or argued about whether it was a loan at all.

Professional Sign-Off Required: corporate counsel for the loan and security documents, and a tax advisor on the interest terms.

The beginner mistake

Moving money between companies by bank transfer with a note that says "loan" and nothing else. A second mistake is charging no interest, or interest that is never paid, without asking a tax advisor what that means for each company. A third is forgetting that the bank's postponement may stop the related lender from being repaid at all until the bank is paid out.

How you will use it

Keep a template loan agreement and a template resolution for intercompany loans, prepared once by your lawyer. Every time money moves between your companies, use them, even for small amounts and short periods.

Keep an intercompany loan register: lender, borrower, date, amount, rate, repayment date, security and registration number. Have your accountant confirm that both companies' books agree with the register at every year-end. When a lender asks for your group's financial picture, the register answers in minutes.
checklist: Write a loan agreement or promissory note for every intercompany loan.
Set the amount, interest, repayment date and default terms.
Approve the loan by resolution in both companies and record conflicts.
Take and register security if the loan matters.
Read any postponement or subordination the bank requires.
Ask a tax advisor about the interest terms.
Keep an intercompany loan register that matches both sets of books.

selftest.q: Your Opco transferred 150,000 to your new Propco six months ago to cover a deposit. There is no document. The Propco is now applying for a construction loan. What should you do?
selftest.a: Document it now, accurately. Decide with your advisors whether it was intended as a loan or a capital contribution, because each has different tax and legal effects. If it was a loan, prepare a loan agreement or promissory note that records the date the money was actually advanced, the interest and the repayment terms, and approve it by resolution in both companies, recording any director's interest. Do not backdate documents to pretend they were signed earlier; record today's date of signing and the earlier date of the advance. Expect the construction lender to require the Opco to postpone the loan. Professional Sign-Off Required: corporate counsel and a tax advisor.

apply: List every amount that has moved between your companies in the last two years. For each, note whether there is a signed agreement, a resolution and matching entries in both sets of books. Send the gaps to your lawyer and accountant.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada), RSC 1985, c 1 (5th Supp), paragraph 20(1)(c) (interest deductibility), subsection 15(2) (shareholder loans) and section 80.4 (deemed interest benefit), named at the level of concepts only; their conditions are detailed and must be confirmed with a tax advisor. Registration of security over personal property is governed by provincial personal property security legislation [specific Act and requirements unverified — confirm independently]. Priority between secured and unsecured creditors is described as a general concept. Section references are cited from the author's working knowledge and should be read on the official Justice Laws website, in the current consolidation, before being relied on. All figures are hypothetical. Education only.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: corporate counsel for the loan and security documents, and a tax advisor on the interest terms.

title: Operating discipline: separate books, separate bank, no commingling
summary: A Holdco and Opco structure only protects you if the companies are actually run as separate businesses: their own bank accounts, their own books and documented dealings with each other and with you. This lesson sets out the daily habits that keep the structure real.
body:
Bottom line. A structure on paper is only as strong as the way it is run. Every company needs its own bank account, its own books, its own contracts and documented dealings with every related party, including you. Commingling, which means mixing the money of different people or companies, is the most common way owners weaken the protection they paid to build.

In plain English

Mr Shabazz, the last four lessons described a wall between companies and between you and your companies. A wall made of documents works only if daily behaviour matches the documents. If one company pays another's bills, if the Opco card pays for your family holiday, or if rent from a property company lands in the Holdco account with no record, the separation becomes hard to prove.

That matters in four places. In a lawsuit, a claimant may argue the companies were really one business. In a tax review, payments for personal expenses can be treated as income to you. A lender wants clean books before it lends. And a buyer will reduce the price, or walk away, if it cannot tell what belongs to the company it is buying.

Operating discipline is not glamorous. It is a set of small, repeated habits. Those habits are what make the structure hold when it is tested.

The framework

  1. One company, one bank account. Each company has its own operating account in its own name. No company pays another's bills directly.
  2. One company, one set of books. Each company has its own accounting file, with its own chart of accounts and year-end.
  3. Intercompany transactions are documented. Loans have loan agreements. Services have written agreements, such as a management agreement with a stated fee. Each transaction has an invoice or a resolution and matching entries in both companies.
  4. Dealings with you are documented. Salary goes through payroll. Dividends are declared by resolution. Money you take or lend is recorded in a shareholder loan account. A personal expense paid by a company can be treated as a taxable benefit to you under subsection 15(1) of the Income Tax Act (Canada), or as a shareholder loan with its own rules.
  5. Contracts in the right name. Each contract, permit application and insurance policy names the company that actually carries the activity.
  6. Monthly reconciliation. Each month, reconcile each bank account and the intercompany balances. Small errors caught monthly are cheap. The same errors found at year-end are expensive.
  7. Signing authority. Record who may sign for each company and up to what amount.

A worked example

Hypothetical. A developer runs a Holdco, an Opco and two Propcos. Over one year, the Opco card pays 40,000 of personal expenses, the Opco pays 60,000 of one Propco's consultant invoices, and rent of 8,000 a month from the other Propco's tenant is deposited into the Holdco's account.

At year-end, the accountant has to untangle it. The 40,000 must be treated as salary, a dividend, a shareholder loan or a taxable benefit, each with a different tax result for the developer and the company. The 60,000 must become a documented intercompany loan or a recharge. The 96,000 of rent belongs to the Propco and must be recorded as owed to it by the Holdco.

The accounting cost is the smaller problem. The larger one is that if the first Propco is ever sued, the claimant has a record showing the companies paid each other's bills and shared accounts, which supports an argument that they were one business.

The disciplined version costs very little: personal costs on a personal card, each Propco paying its own consultants, rent paid into the Propco's own account, and a monthly reconciliation.

Professional Sign-Off Required: the company's accountant to correct the records, and a tax advisor on the personal expenses.

The beginner mistake

Using whichever account has money in it today. It feels efficient. It creates a year-end clean-up, a tax exposure and a weaker structure. The second mistake is fixing it all at year-end with journal entries and no supporting documents, which is less credible than a record made at the time. A third mistake is letting one trusted employee move money between all the companies without a second person ever reviewing it.

How you will use it

Run a simple monthly routine for each company: reconcile the bank account, review every payment to or from a related company or to you, and confirm each one has a document. Thirty minutes a month per company is enough once the habit is set.

Give your bookkeeper one written rule: no company pays another company's or a person's expense without a document that says why. When a payment goes the wrong way by mistake, correct it the same month with a documented reimbursement. A structure that is run this way is one you can show to a lender, a buyer, a tax auditor or a court with confidence.

Review the structure itself once a year with your accountant: are there companies that no longer do anything, accounts that are no longer needed, or intercompany balances that have grown with no plan to repay them? Closing what is not needed keeps the discipline manageable.
checklist: Give each company its own bank account in its own name.
Keep separate books for each company.
Document every intercompany loan, service and payment.
Run salary, dividends and shareholder loans through proper records.
Keep personal expenses off company cards.
Reconcile bank accounts and intercompany balances monthly.
Record who may sign for each company and the limits.

selftest.q: Your Opco's account is low this week, so you pay a 25,000 Opco supplier invoice from your Holdco's account. What should happen next?
selftest.a: Record it immediately as what it is. The usual approach is to treat it as a loan from the Holdco to the Opco: record the 25,000 as owing in both companies' books, and cover it under a written intercompany loan agreement or an existing loan facility approved by resolution. Then repay it, or confirm its terms, at the next reconciliation. Better still, in future have the Holdco lend the money to the Opco's account first, so the Opco pays its own supplier. Ask your tax advisor whether interest should be charged. Professional Sign-Off Required: the company's accountant, and a tax advisor on the loan terms.

apply: For one company, review last month's bank statement. Mark every payment to or from another company you own, or to you personally. For each, write down the supporting document, or write "missing".
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada), RSC 1985, c 1 (5th Supp), subsection 15(1) (shareholder benefits), named as a concept only; how a given payment is treated depends on facts and must be confirmed with a tax advisor. The link between commingling and arguments that companies should be treated as one is a general concept, not a fixed legal test [confirm independently with counsel]. Section references are cited from the author's working knowledge and should be read on the official Justice Laws website, in the current consolidation, before being relied on. All figures are hypothetical. Education only.
